One business stands out at Home Depot (HD): SRS, an acquisition that now sells through Home Depot's stores and that bulls may be betting on. You probably see Home Depot as a store chain tied to housing. Management says housing turnover has been low for four years, and Home Depot stock lost 16.9% over the past year, while the S&P 500 gained 16.5%. That is the contradiction: a business that may be growing faster than the rest of Home Depot sits inside a stock that has trailed the market. So is SRS really growing faster than the rest of Home Depot?

SRS Is Outgrowing The Rest Of Home Depot

So far, yes. During the quarter that ended August 2, 2026, SRS grew its comparable sales faster than Home Depot as a whole. Overall comparable sales for the company rose 1.7%. SRS was positive in all of its verticals, and management said on the August 18, 2026 call that it looks to be taking significant share.

Management expects SRS to keep growing for the year. It guided the business to mid-single-digit organic sales growth for fiscal 2026. For the whole company, management guided a different measure, comparable sales growth of flat to 2%.

One number shows how far SRS has spread: 90%. That is the share of Home Depot's stores that closed a sale through SRS within the last 12 months, management said, so SRS no longer sits apart from the stores.

Home Depot's Margin Has Slipped For Three Years

Home Depot's profit has not kept up with SRS's growth so far. Its operating margin was 14.9% over the twelve months that ended July 30, 2023. The figure slipped to 13.9% a year later. Operating margin fell again to 13.1% in the twelve months to August 3, 2025 and to 12.4% in the twelve months to August 2, 2026. That marks the lowest rate at any of the past 40 quarter ends.

The latest quarter's gross margin looked better, and that is where the worry sits. On the same call, the question came up whether Home Depot would have missed profit forecasts without a tariff refund. Management said the company would have beaten its own expectations regardless. By management's count, the refund added about 145 basis points to gross margin, yet gross margin rose only about 25 basis points from a year earlier. About 60 basis points of it went to higher fuel, energy and input costs, and about 60 more went to the mix of the GMS and Mingledorff's acquisitions.

Home Depot does get more sales from those acquisitions. Management expects total sales to grow about 2.5% to 4.5% in fiscal 2026, reflecting the GMS acquisition, new stores, new branches and tuck-in acquisitions. But management also expects the unplanned input costs to fully offset the tariff refunds over the year.

Target (TGT) stock rose 73.2% over the past year. That marks the biggest gain in a group of six retailers that includes Walmart and Costco. Yet Target still costs less against its earnings than any of those rivals. The price appears to assume Target's sales will keep trailing most of its rivals and its margin, helped by tariff refunds, will not hold. So how much less are you paying, and what do you get for it?

What You Get For Target's Lower Price

You pay far less. Target trades at 15.8 times its earnings over its past four quarters, against 42.4 times for Walmart in the same retail industry.

For that lower price, you get a business that keeps more of each sales dollar as operating profit. Target posts 5.6%, compared with 4.4% for Walmart. In return, you give up growth: Target's sales rose 2.0% over its past four quarters, while Walmart's rose 6.2%.

Amazon, Costco and Home Depot also trade at a higher P/E than Target and grow sales faster. Target's margin sits above Costco's, but Amazon and Home Depot earn higher margins at 12.1% and 12.4%.

Target's margin lead over Walmart holds so far, but most of it came from tariff refunds. In the quarter that ended August 1, 2026, tariff refunds added 3.7 percentage points to Target's 9.6% operating margin, management said on the August 19 call. Without them, the operating margin would have been 5.9%, against 5.2% a year earlier. Excluding the refunds, management said the gross margin rose about 1 percentage point from a year earlier as Target lapped heavy markdowns and grew its higher-margin revenue streams.

Which Parts Of Target's Business Are Growing?

Target's sales are growing again, but two large categories are lagging. Sales rose 5.3% from a year earlier in the quarter that ended August 1. This marked the second rise in a row following a fall in the quarter that ended January 31.

Management said comparable sales rose 3.8%, driven by more shoppers. It said traffic rose 3.6%, and the average purchase was about flat. Online sales grew faster than store sales, led by more than 25% growth in same-day delivery.

title: Ulta Beauty's website traffic just surged a whopping 48%

Ulta Beauty's website traffic just surged a whopping 48%
Tobi Opeyemi Amure, Dana Sullivan Kilroy

ULTA
TGT
AMZN
KSS
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

If you shop for beauty products, you have more choices than ever. Sephora sits inside Kohl's, Amazon sells prestige brands, and Target went all-in on its own beauty push after its split with Ulta, as TheStreet reported.

That crowded field has made investors nervous about Ulta for most of 2026. The worry is simple: if shoppers can find the same lipstick anywhere, why make the trip?

Ulta is still growing anyway. Net sales rose 8.9% to $3.04 billion in the second quarter, and comparable sales climbed 3.8%, according to the company's earnings release dated Aug. 27.

"Our team delivered another impressive quarter of strong sales, profit, and earnings growth," CEO Kecia Steelman said in the release.

However, Wall Street wanted proof that growth would hold up in the back half of the year, when the comparisons get harder.

According to a Bank of America research report reviewed by TheStreet, that proof may already be showing up on Ulta's website. Visits to Ulta.com jumped 48% from a year earlier in September, the bank said, citing Similarweb data.

Ulta Beauty's rising online traffic fuels holiday sales optimism, prompting Bank of America to raise its price target.Stefanie Keenan / Getty Images
What Bank of America found in Ulta's web traffic

The September jump wasn't a one-off. Site visits rose 38% through the first nine months of the year, with growth above 30% every month since April, wrote BofA analyst Lorraine Hutchinson in the Oct. 20 note, titled "Higher web traffic creates opportunity for 2H comp upside." That is a long streak for a retailer whose stock was punished over growth fears just two months ago.

"Consumers are engaged, and we are optimistic about ULTA's ability to convert this higher traffic into sales," Hutchinson wrote.

Digital sales have grown at a rate between the low double digits and the mid-teens in recent quarters, the bank said, yet they make up only about 20% of revenue. Steelman said on the August call that e-commerce posted its "sixth consecutive quarter of double-digit sales growth," according to the Motley Fool transcript.

Related: Ulta Beauty's move to win back shoppers takes a new turn

That's where the bank sees upside. Ulta's guidance implies second-half comparable sales growth of 2% to 3%, and Chief Financial Officer Chris DelOrefice confirmed that range on the call.

The stock has already moved. Shares fell about 3% to $524 in after-hours trading on Aug. 27 as investors fretted about slowing growth, Investing.com reported. By Oct. 20, they stood at $591.62, according to the BofA note, a gain of roughly 13% by my math.

Beauty spending keeps beating the rest of retail

The broader category is giving Ulta room to run. Prestige beauty sales rose 7% to $17.1 billion in the first half of 2026, and mass beauty climbed 7% to $39.2 billion, according to Circana on Aug. 11.

title: How much MSFT stock does Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella actually own?
detail:
How much MSFT stock does Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella actually own?
Laura Rodini, Jeremy Salvucci
Thu, October 22, 2026 at 10:07 AM MST 4 min read
MSFT
NOK
OPAI.PVT
AAPL
GOOG
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Not many people remember this, but when Satya Nadella took the reins as CEO of Microsoft in February 2014, the company was struggling to find its place amidst a tech landscape dominated by Apple's smartphones, Google's Android operating system, and Amazon's cloud computing services.

Under the leadership of Steve Ballmer, Microsoft had undertaken a contentious $7.2 billion acquisition of Nokia's mobile phone business in 2013. That deal ultimately failed, resulting in billions in write-downs and thousands of layoffs.

But Nadella did not turn the company around overnight. Over the next few years, he shifted Microsoft's business model even further into cloud computing by expanding Azure and its subscription-based services. He also made strategic acquisitions, including LinkedIn, GitHub, and Minecraft, while investing billions into artificial intelligence before it became a household name.

In fact, you could say that Nadella was instrumental in Microsoft's partnership with OpenAI, as he even personally stepped in to serve as mediator when OpenAI's board briefly fired its CEO and co-founder, Sam Altman, in the fall of 2023.

Although Microsoft and OpenAI renegotiated their once-exclusive partnership, Microsoft hasn't lost momentum. Their newest agreement, announced in April 2026, gave each greater independence and allowed Microsoft to continue to expand its own AI capabilities through Azure's cloud services.

MSFT crossed the trillion-dollar valuation threshold on April 25, 2019, and it hasn't looked back since. In its most recent earnings, the company reported that Azure revenue grew by 43% year-over-year. These results show that Microsoft isn't just one of the founders of the digital era — it's very much a power player, and as the driver behind its innovation, Nadella himself has been rewarded handsomely through salary increases, bonuses, and enormous stock awards.

How much of MSFT does Satya Nadella own? Is he the biggest inividual shareholder?

As of Microsoft's latest Proxy statement for fiscal 2025, filed in September 2025, Satya Nadella owned 900,572 shares of Microsoft, equating to about 0.01% of the company's total outstanding shares.

Given MSFT's October 19 closing share price of $533.52, those shares would be worth a whopping $480.4 million.

But Nadella isn't Microsoft's biggest individual shareholder — not by a long shot.

That distinction actually belongs to Steve Ballmer, who is estimated to still own approximately 319 million shares, or roughly 4% of Microsoft. Despite Ballmer stepping down amid Microsoft's struggles, he still owns more than 350 times as much as Nadella's stake.
